extracted.intended_audience: politically engaged literate public, lawyers, and legislators (18th-century England)
extracted.subtask_short: critique of judicial conduct and bail law
extracted.subtask_description: A series of political-legal letters arguing standards for judicial conduct, the limits of judicial discretion (especially re: bail), the rights of juries and the press, and broader constitutional/policy principles in 18th-century England.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial adherence to precedent; limits on judicial innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges should not introduce new modes of proceeding or new law, nor remove landmarks established by former decisions; converting a court of common law into a court of equity (or otherwise changing its system of jurisprudence) is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that Lord Mansfield 'laboured to introduce new modes of proceeding' and 'to change a court of common law into a court of equity,' warning that such innovations risk enabling future injustice and place too much power in a single judge. The public must judge between adhering to precedent and judicial novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive life tenure for judges (not merely symbolic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative provisions establishing judges 'for life' must confer real security and not be mere appearances that leave power effectively unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The letter criticises a bill that only prevents removal by a successor of the king and calls that a 'legacy, not a gift,' arguing the provision conferred no meaningful concession by the sovereign and thus lacks the substance to secure judicial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish legal status of general warrants and press-warrants by formal decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of illegality should rest on formal judicial decisions; while general warrants were tried and declared illegal, press-warrants have been complained of but have not seen a formal decision against them in superior courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author insists one cannot equate the two without recognizing that general warrants were 'regularly questioned or resisted' and declared illegal at trial, whereas press-warrants, though resisted and complained of, have been recognized and admitted by Parliament and supported by some judicial opinions. Comparisons without such formal foundation are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance individual liberty with public safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrates defending individual liberty must also consider and provide for the safety of the community; limitations on liberty may be justified when necessary for public defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to impressment: in times of foreign war or threat of invasion, the state may need to man the fleet even at cost to some individual liberty; the magistrate must weigh individual rights against communal safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of necessity is limited to inevitable circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessity implies inevitability and, only in such cases, creates a law to which positive laws and rights must give way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the levy of ship money by the king's warrant was not 'necessary' because Parliament could have acted; therefore the necessity doctrine cannot be used to justify executive acts that are avoidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impressment should be confined strictly to seamen; pressing others is abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of pressing (impressment) must be confined to seamen in times of public danger; pressing persons other than seamen is a gross abuse that magistrates can and should correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Junius explicitly confines his argument 'strictly to seamen' and calls pressing of others a gross abuse. The magistrate's corrective role is emphasised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of juries to return a general verdict is constitutional and needs no bill
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of juries to return a general verdict in all cases is a part of the constitution and requires no legislative enactment either enacting or declaratory to confirm it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author urges Englishmen to 'stand upon his guard' against attempts to erode jury rights and warns that an asserted need for a confirming bill is misplaced because the right is inherent in the constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial doctrines must not be legitimized by hiding behind legislative acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges should not attempt to shelter unconstitutional doctrines by attributing them to or hiding them behind an act of the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that Lord Mansfield's policy of 'screening his unconstitutional doctrines behind an act of the legislature' should be resisted and that citizens must be vigilant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws must be proportionate and preserve trial by jury (critique of game laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation (here, the game laws) must not be oppressive: penalties should be proportionate to the offence, modes of trial must preserve the benefits of trial by jury, and statutes must avoid summary, arbitrary procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Junius characterises the game laws and recent acts (e.g., to prevent dog stealing or killing between sun and sun) as 'absurd, extravagant, and pernicious,' asserting that their penal provisions and trial modes deprive subjects of legal liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of King's Bench to bail for felony must be grounded in statute, not mere practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The asserted superior power of the court of King's Bench to bail in felony cases is said to be founded on lawyers' opinion and practice; legislative assent is merely negative and not supported by any explicit positive statutory provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author challenges defenders to produce a statute authorising this power and promises to analyse the relevant statutes in detail. He frames the King's Bench power as a creature of practice rather than express statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial discretion must be exercised according to law and legislative intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Discretion is legitimate only when directed by the law's right line and the spirit, intent, and meaning of the legislature; discretion that is arbitrary, capricious, or not so directed is unlawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting authoritative jurists (e.g., 'Discretion... is, discernere per legem quid sit justum' and 'Novelties, without warrant of precedents, are not to be allowed'), the text insists judges are not free to create novelties and must follow established rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persons taken in flagrante with stolen goods are not bailable
rubrics_metrics.description: A person positively charged with felony and taken in the act (with stolen goods upon him) should not be bailable; the law treats such a person as essentially equivalent to a convict and accepts no security other than confinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asserts this as the indisputable meaning of the legislature, supports it with historical common-law practice (e.g., 'taken with the maner' approximating conviction), and proposes to cite statutes (e.g., Westminster I) to prove the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of favourable circumstances means no bail for felony
rubrics_metrics.description: If no favourable circumstances are alleged to lessen the force of the evidence (e.g., when a prisoner is taken in the fact with the stolen goods and makes no defence), then even a lord chief justice has no more right to grant bail than a justice of the peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains how alleged favourable circumstances change the prisoner's legal state; absent such allegations, the presumption from the statutory/common-law framework is against bail.

rubrics_metrics.name: A judge's prior abuse of power cannot justify the same abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: A judge's previous illegal or improper acts (e.g., bailing for manifest crimes) do not justify those acts as lawful; one judge's example is no legal defence for repeating or endorsing the wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author rejects the argument 'you have often bailed for murders, rapes...' as a defence; precedent of judicial misconduct does not become a lawful practice by repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of bail law requires reference to statutes (e.g., Westminster I)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of bail in charges of felony has been exactly ascertained by acts of the legislature and must be interpreted with direct reference to the relevant statutes rather than by loose common-law assertion alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author indicates he will 'state, in due order, the several statutes relative to bail in criminal cases' (omitting superfluous words) and argues this statutory history is decisive for the question at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate etiquette: answer arguments in their own words and avoid appeals to passion
rubrics_metrics.description: In disputation, take an opponent's argument in their own words and answer it strictly; comparisons may sometimes illustrate but do not prove, and appeals to the passions are unfair and unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Junius admonishes critics to avoid vague comparisons and passion-based rebuttals, offering that he will 'show himself ready to concur in any rational plan' and expects issues not be exaggerated or misrepresented.
